claims.text: The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi changes the stacking-fault energy of the resulting FeNiCrMn alloy.
Removing Co changes dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
The Co-free alloy undergoes more dynamic recovery than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The Co-free alloy has higher strain-rate sensitivity than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The modified atomic configuration permits easier thermally activated dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
The modified atomic configuration reinforces dislocation entanglement at lower temperatures.
Lattice distortion and local chemical inhomogeneity affect mobile dislocations and stacking-fault structures.
A change in stacking-fault energy changes the balance between dislocation glide and mechanical twinning.
A change in stacking-fault energy changes the balance between dislocation glide and cross-slip.
At lower temperatures, enhanced dislocation interactions produce steeper strain hardening in the Co-free alloy.
At lower temperatures, the Co-free alloy has a higher initial strain-hardening rate than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
At lower temperatures, the Co-free alloy has a higher yield strength than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation facilitates dynamic recovery in the Co-free alloy.
Dynamic recovery maintains ductility by reducing the rate of work softening.
At elevated temperatures, the Co-free alloy exhibits less rapid thermal softening than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed predictions are intended to apply from room temperature to approximately 900 degrees Celsius within the elastic-plastic tensile-deformation regime.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes enhanced dynamic recovery at elevated temperature but also predicts that this recovery causes less rapid thermal or work softening. The proposed direction of the recovery-to-softening link is internally unclear and is not reconciled by an additional strengthening mechanism.
